title: The Legion of the Damned roars back into Warhammer 40k in Kill Team Armageddon
content:
On Friday, just as the Warhammer Big Autumn Preview was winding down, Games Workshop brought out the big guns - brand new models for the Legion of the Damned. There's much to be said about these mysterious and ethereal Space Marines, but for the benefit of anyone who hasn't been stewing in the hobby for a long time, the short version is this - they're angry ghosts who are always on fire.

The new Legion of the Damned kits will debut in Warhammer 40k Kill Team: Armageddon, the next big box release for the tactical skirmish game. They're paired up against an mob of Ork Nobz and their weedy gretchin accomplices, and they'll do battle against the background of new Kill Zone Armageddon terrain.

The new Legion of the Damned models are, if you'll permit me to be poetic, freaking sick. The new kit is packed with references to the various earlier models and pieces of art that have represented them, and they're wearing a motley mixture of different power armor, including Mk VII and Mk VI.

GW has confirmed that the Legion will have rules in 40k, though not where those will show up. In Kill Team there are several models with special roles, including a Legionnaire ancient equipped with a flaming skeleton banner, a gunner with a meltagun, and an incinerator with a heavy flamer. The overall effect is absolutely freaking metal.

1/4

The Nob mob was revealed in the run up to the new Ork Codex release. In 40k they're a bit of a melee and ranged blender unit, but in Kill Team they'll function a little differently. See, every Nob in the mob thinks they're the boss, and their rules will give each one main character energy. A pair of gretchin - which are just tokens in 40k - will here provide some much needed extra activations for the elite Kill Team.

The new Kill Zone Armageddon terain is rather tasty. The most basic items in it are pieces of ruined Frontieris terrain - smashed up versions of earlier boxy Kill Team bits - but there's plenty of very interesting new stuff, including a ruined Rogal Dorn, a wrecked Redemptor Dreadnought - with a removable sarcophagus for a rescue mission objective - and two bunkers that models can fit inside (admittedly, not many models, given the size of the combatants).

1/3

The Legion of the Damned have been part of 40k lore since 1988, and they've had model kits on and off ever since. These apparitions appear without warning during seemingly hopeless battles, often coming to the aid of other loyalist Space Marine chapters, smiting the Emperor's enemies and then disappearing without a trace. And at the current moment in the lore, there are few places where Space Marines need more help than the war world of Armageddon…

If you want to dive into the lore for the Legion of the Damned, I wrote up a comprehensive guide covering every major theory for what they actually are since their first write up in White Dwarf magazine.

title: Warhammer 40k lore - the Legion of the Damned, loyalists lost in the warp
content:
The Legion of the Damned might be the closest that Warhammer 40,000 gets to the cover art of a heavy metal album. Take the brutally metal concept of a Space Marine Chapter, holy warriors in ceramite power armor wielding military chainsaws and rapid firing grenade launchers, then make them ghosts and set them on fire - that's the Legion of the Damned. But who are these mysterious warriors, and what's the story behind that heavy metal facade?

The Legion of the Damned debuted in 1988's White Dwarf episode 99, in an article by Rick Priestley, but it was 1995's Codex Ultramarines - the closest thing to a generic Codex Space Marines for Warhammer 40k 2nd edition - that introduced them in the form we recognise them today. This description is still very apt: "In times of great adversity, the Legion will come to the aid of Space Marines in battle, turning defeat into victory" - afterward, "The Legion vanishes, leaving no trace of their presence or clues as to their origin".

A short story in the voice of Ultramarines Chief Librarian Tigurius describes their arrival and appearance. Tigurius' forces are on the verge of annihilation by Orks, and - with the company chaplain dead - he leads the troops in prayer on the eve of the final battle. When he raises his head from his prayers, a host of mysterious marines have entered the fray.

"Their armor was colored black and upon it was drawn chilling images of bones and fire, and on their helms they bore skulls" - pretty gnarly couture for loyalist marines in 1995, since the Blood Angels Death Company and Mortifactors didn't yet exist in their modern forms. "As they advanced an eerie glow shrouded them and fire seemed to dance about their feet", Tigurius continues, "Like the bones of men in the torment of purgatory they were, so that they looked more like skeletons than living men. Yet not a sound did they make".

Loyalist ghost marines, then. The Legion of the Damned may have been inspired by the 1914 short story 'The Bowmen' by Arthur Machen, a tale set during the Great War in which a host of ghostly archers from the battle of Agincourt are summoned by a British soldier praying to Saint George, saving his company. Machen's story was likely inspired by the recent British victory at the Battle of Mons - and his tale would, in turn, inspire the popular myth of the 'Angel of Mons' protecting the British during that battle.

Like many things published during the first edition of Warhammer 40k, Priestley's article lays out in very explicit detail things that later lore would change to supposition and myth. Priestley identifies the Legion of the Damned as the Fire Hawks chapter. In 963.M41 the entire Fire Hawks chapter fleet, including its fortress monastery, was lost in the warp when it attempted a translation to the Crows World sub-sector. After 20 years the wider Imperium declared them dead.

Of course the Fire Hawks weren't totally gone. In this version of the lore,  the Legion was driven to near madness by a warp-borne wasting disease that doomed them to an agonising death, while simultaneously heightening their strength. They fought on in service of the Imperium, but had begun to completely break down as a Space Marine chapter.

Newer versions of the lore are a lot more ghostly and less corporeal, perhaps because the agonising warp-borne disease angle became integral to the backstory for the Death Guard. The sixth edition supplement Codex: Legion of the Damned does include the suggestion that they are the lost Fire Hawks chapter, but it's now presented as one theory among several.

One theory, purported by the radical Inquisitor Quixos, is that humanity's faith in the Emperor had given rise to literal warp entities under his control, functionally speaking daemons. Some scholars believe that they are manifestations of the powers of Space Marine Librarians, drawing upon the psychic backlash of traumatic historical events like "the Isstvan massacres or the death of a Primarch" - which might explain why the Legion only appears where Space Marines are present. Radicals believe they may actually be psychic manifestations of the great mass of humanity, which - given the current Psychic Awakening in the Imperium - may explain why they've been sighted more in recent years. And a quote from an Eldar Autarch says they are simply Daemons.

The warp sickness explanation reappears as Quadrimesta's Thesis of Perpetual Martyrdom, which posits the marines have "somehow blended with the stuff of the Warp, contracting a kind of metaphysical contagion", which they are attempting to protect the rest of the Imperium from. Unlike the original version of the disease, this is hypothesised to allow them to be "reborn after a certain period of time, much as a banished Daemon can return to the service of its masters after its purgatory is complete". This connection to the Warp allows the Legion to read the Emperor's Tarot with uncanny accuracy, which is why its interventions always arrive at the last, most critical moment. But the Legion is trapped in a cycle of impurity, constantly seeking ways to strike against the foes of the Imperium to earn a redemption which its contaminated state will never permit.

While the Imperium isn't sure what the Legion of the Damned is, it has too many other things to worry about to actively pursue them as enemies. And the Legion appears to be loyal. In the battle for Cadia during the 13th Black Crusade, the Legion assisted in the assault that destroyed the power core of a Blackstone Fortress; since the fall of Cadia, and particularly during the Noctis Aeterna when the light of the Astronomicon was temporarily extinguished, they have been sighted on worlds across the Imperium.

Is Ferrus Manus in the Legion of the Damned?

Ferrus Manus, the Primarch of the Iron Hands Space Marine Legion, was slain by his brother Fulgrim during the dropsite massacre on Istvaan IV. His ghost appeared in the penultimate Horus Heresy Book, The End and the Death: Volume II, speaking to the Primarch Sanguinius - but this occurred when warp energy had entirely saturated the material realm. Fans have made some excellent fan art about a blazing ghostly version of Ferrus Manus as part of the Legion of the Damned, but there's no lore connection at all. If you want to make a conversion, though, more power to you!

For a great community that loves Warhammer 40k lore deep dives, hop into the Wargamer Discord community. And for a weekly roundup of our biggest articles, make sure you're signed up to our regular newsletter.

title: Warhammer 40k Adeptus Custodes codex revealed, alongside massive new terminators
content:
On Friday, during the Big Warhammer Autumn Preview, Games Workshop had some massive reveals for the Adeptus Custodes; a packed new codex for Warhammer 40k, massive new terminators, and unit stats that make even Space Marine captains look positively weedy.

The Custodes will be the next Warhammer 40k codex release after the Space Marines, who go up for pre-order on Sunday September 19th. GW spokesperson Eddie Eccles says that "most" of the existing 40k Custodes units will be available in the army, while all of the new Horus Heresy plastic kits will make the leap.

They're joined by brand new plastic Aquilon Terminators, replacing some long-serving resin kits from the Horus Heresy. In 40k they divide up into two different units based on variant loadouts: equipped with either vehicle-smashing Solarite Power Gauntlets, or infantry-eviscerating Solarite Power Talons. They then get a choice of Infernus Firepikes or Lastrum Storm Bolters.

If you field them in the Heresy you can equip them with a mix and match selection of weaponry, as before. Their Heresy rules will appear in the upcoming Journal Tactica 'The Battle for the Signus Cluster: Assault on Kol', which will also feature rules for Slaaneshi daemon armies and Slaaneshi afflicted Solar Auxilia.

Though Custodian armies will have a bigger range of models to choose from, the size of armies will be a lot smaller. The recently upgraded Space Marines might seem tough, but the Custodians are absolute monsters. The most basic Custodian guardian now has T7 and 5W - on top of that classic 2+/4++ save - and those new terminators? Toughness eight, with six wounds.

GW is releasing a new Custodes Combat Patrol alongside the Codex. While this has about as many models as you'd expect to find in this sort of box set - three flying Venatarii, a Sodality of six Custodian Guard, a Shield Captain, and a Dreadnought. But they're so powerful that in games of Combat Patrol, you'll only actually field half of this set at a time.

I'm an uppie downie shooty army with charge from 6" DS.

My detachment rule is to re-roll 1s to hit, and to make tunnels:

- The Red Terror and the Mawlocs make a 40mm tunnel marker within 1" when they arrive from DS.

- Other units in reserve can DS wholly within 9" of tunnel markers, and then arrive outside 6" of your units.

- Charging is allowed.

- If on of your units end a move within 3" of a tunnel marker it dies.

My strats are, in order of importance:

- Uppie downie, either both Mawlocs or any one unit

- On board teleport between tunnels

- Sus 1 and ignore cover on unit arriving from reserves

- 6" re-roll charge aura on a monster that arrived from reserves

- Heal/rez d3+1 wholly within 9" of a tunnel

- Synapse on a Mawloc

Important tricks:

- The Red Terror has innate uppie downie if unenganged, on _both_ player's turns

- Swarmy has vect

- Maleceptors have a 6" aura of -1 to hit, also -1 to wound if you are below half strength.

- Neurolictors cause a command phase BS test within 12", and give battle-shocked units within 12" -1 to hit and +1 to be wounded.

- On arriving from DS, Mawlocs roll a d6 for each unit within 12" and deal mortals. 1: nothing, 2-4: d3, 5+: 3 and a BS test.

Welcome back, Dear Reader, to my ongoing blog of hobby and competitive play progress through 2026. Yesterday I wrote about the first two days of my time at Challengers Cup - arriving at the event and the first day of games. Today I'm diving right into days 2 and 3 of the event, talking about the rest of my games and our final finish. Please avoid checking ahead and wait until I'm done to find out how we did, thanks.

Saturday: Trying (and Failing) to go 0-0-6

Saturday starts with a solid breakfast. We bought a dozen eggs the night before, so I scramble those up and heat up the leftover taco meat and refried beans to make tacos. Now, a good breakfast taco really needs potatoes, but all of our potatoes were more or less reserved for dinner Saturday night, so we go with what we have. Which includes some store-bought pico de gallo.

That said, the tacos are a great starting point for the day, and we also have some leftover donuts delivered by Kelling's wife. Then it's a pair of trips back over to the venue for rounds three and four.

Max's list is a Carnival of Excess list running Fulgrim, which is interesting. My goal is to generally stay the hell away from it and let him come to me a few models at a time, taking down bigger targets as they make their way onto the table. Shalaxi is a problem, but not a massive one in the way Fulgrim is.

This game had one of my favorite moments of the weekend: In an effort to get an early Assassination kill and lock me in my deployment zone, Max sends a unit of Infractors and a Lord Exultant across the table to try and kill my Tzaangor Shaman and one of my Rubric units. I throw out some limited Overwatch at them, killing 2 models. Then he closes the gap on a big charge, and I drop the combat grenade, killing two more models and leaving just one Infractor and the Lord. The Lord activates his once-per-game "best day ever" mode and drops six 3-damage precision wounds on my Infernal Master, who rolls four 5+ saves. Then I flip one of the two fails to a 6 to survive on 1 wound. Meanwhile the Infractor doesn't kill the Shaman. They turn around and kill both models, giving me a solid start on the game.

This one goes really well early for me - Max feeds me all of his Infractors, Flawless Blades, and Noise Marines without getting much in return - and then turns disastrously late when I set up wrong for my Rituals on Fulgrim and fail the double move and re-roll casts, leaving me unable to dump shots into him until he's dead. That ends up being a brutal turn as I'm staring down Shalaxi and Fulgrim at the same time at the top of the board. I failed half my casts again the following turn, and while I was able to kill Fulgrim, the damage was done. Max draws a stellar final turn with Forward Position and Assassination and scores 15 on Secondaries and while I have second turn advantage and pull 15 of my own, I needed to stop him from being able to just trivially pick up units for Overwhelming Force and Assassination.

The game ends up being an 82-84 loss for me and a 10-10 draw but it definitely could have been a 12 if I'd been able to close out Fulgrim earlier with a double move. Our team would end up winning the round, 85-75, giving us our first round win of the event and killing our dreams of 0-0-6. Max was a treat to play and so was the rest of Tabletop Hawaii.

Lunch was more manageable on day 2, and I ended up getting a burrito from the place I'd had to cancel with the day before. It was aggressively mid, rolled in that way where all the meant is on one side of the thing and I started with the side that was apparently all cilantro and sour cream. Gross.

This game was a little awkward at first but picked up quickly. Jerred was a fun opponent and we had a solid game. The problem with Votann is that they just generally cost too much for what you get, and so most games go the same way: I kill things reliably until turn 3, then ask my opponent where the rest of his army is, at which point he'll say "this is it" and I get to be like "damn bitch, you live like this?"

That said, going second into Priority Assets with Purge is never easy. My goal here is to control both center objectives all games with Terminators and avoid taking too much damage from the 10man Hearthguard unit. Jerred screams forward at the start of the game with his Kapricus Carrier, bikes, and Saggitaurs, and I promptly take them all off the board and go to work killing his Yaegirs and Warriors - they're the key here. Votann don't have a lot of units, so what you want to do is force him to have to do actions with the Thunderkyn or the Steeljacks, neither of which want to be doing them and give up a ton of shooting value.

I play aggressively with the Mutalith early and focus on controlling board with my shooting threats for a turn. Jerred gets a single marker on the top center objective but I'm able to hold it for much of the game - he leaves me room to drop Terminators on the middle and I never look back.

Jerred's Hearthguard would ultimately end up dropping on the left side of the table outside of my deployment zone, where they'd clear my home point but be unable to do much else. My Terminators take the middle and spend a few turns getting whittled down by Thunderkyn and Steeljacks while firing back as the other unit wheels around and captures Jerred's expansion. I kept Jerred off primary scoring in rounds 3 and 4 almost completely but he still managed to outscore me on secondary objectives, in part because he drew Secure/Assassination on turn 1 and Cleanse round 2 before finishing round 5 with Bring it Down and No Prisoners.

I'd end up winning this one 12-8 and securing a W for the team. It wasn't super close, but the mission makes it hard to pull away. What also helped me was Jerred not just aggressively castling on one objective; he didn't realize you can keep dropping priority markers on the same objective, which helped me.

We tied the round again, 84-76, and finished the day 1-0-3, still undefeated. I'm honestly OK with these results - we haven't been on the losing end of a draw yet and we've only been a couple points away from wins. We keep getting paired down and that helps us.

Anyways none of this matters because IT IS STEAK NIGHT.

Steak Night

One of the things I try to do at every one of these gatherings is do a night with some steaks. The first day at the grocery store I stopped by their butcher's counter and picked out eight of their best ribeyes and had them wrapped up. I'd prefer filets but they didn't have enough of those. The plan here is almost always "steak and potatoes, plus vegetables." This year I added some mac and cheese, broccoli, and asparagus, and Boon had picked up some naan bread so we heated that up too.

Grilling isn't the ideal way to make steaks, but it's not bad. I do a little salt and Montreal steak seasoning on them, and I've prepared a rosemary garlic butter to finish them off - mince garlic and rosemary, mix into softened butter. I put rosemary on the steaks and cook them about 7 minutes each side while the asparagus also sits on the grill, brushed with salt, pepper, and olive oil. The Broccoli was tossed in olive oil and Montreal steak seasoning, then roasted at 425 for about 20 minutes, and the potatoes were boiled with a clove of crushed garlic, then drained, mashed, and combined with butter and heavy whipping cream.

The steaks were left to rest for about 5 minutes, during which time they got a dollop of garlic rosemary butter. In all it was an impressive spread, and we ended up with like eight pounds of mashed potatoes - I could have definitely used on for breakfast tacos, in retrospect. Overall another successful meal - the steaks turned out beautifully and there was plenty to eat even for Chase. My take is that it's very important to have vegetables at these things - you need to stay healthy and not just eat pizza all weekend.

Sunday: The Struggle to Not Lose

We wake up Sunday with two games to go. Saturday night was probably our best post-dinner hangout, with most everyone engaged and talking about games and pairings before we hit the back deck and spent the rest of the evening debating politics and talking about how trains are rad while looking out over the valley and watching planes land. I think I crashed around midnight again.

Sunday morning was another two-trip morning and this time our first game was upstairs in the bleachers. This meant having a lot of space but also music in the background, which wasn't as bad as it sounds - it was basically top radio hits from the late 90s, which was catnip to my opponent and me. We spent half the game softly singing Sugar Ray and RHCP songs.

We open with Chaos Knights this time around and I get paired into Necrons. Funny enough, I played two members of this team - AJ Edman and Rich Dudley - at the GW US Open in Tacoma earlier this year. I beat AJ en route to the top cut, then lost to Rich playing Necrons on Purge the Foe. This was more or less an exact replay of that, even using the same layout. The big difference? Both of our armies were worse. Rich had one extra C'tan and a unit of fast-moving Lychguard; the Lychguard could catch me by surprise and taking down two C'tan is a tall order. I'm going first in this mission and that sucks - you want to go second here, even with the changes to the "kill more" part of the Purge mirror primary. That first turn going first is often dead for kills, and that would prove to be true here as I tried to play cagey on the first turn.

I tend to play too aggressively most of the time, so a lot of what I'm trying to do in these games is slow down, score where I can, and keep games close. My primary goal was to take the lokhust destroyers out of the equation and avoid the Scarabs. I did the former and failed at the latter. I made a big mistake turn 1 on my end, losing a key model to a failed Hazardous check which cost me the ability to score Centre Ground.

Despite being dumb enough to engage the Scarabs, I did manage to tie them up in the lower corner for the entire game with a unit of Rubrics, also taking out a unit of Lokhusts, though I suspect this was a bad trade on my part - that Wraiths unit costs about 200 points less than my Terminators. I eventually managed to dig out a bit more with the second unit of Terminators, but that was throwing good points after bad - I needed to use them more at midtable.

I was eventually able to take out the Void Dragon with a mix of shooting from the Mutalith and Rubrics, and some clever use of the Chaos Spawn I made from my Terminator Sorcerer and the Rubrics let me drop in and score Plunder and Behind Enemy Lines on the game's final turn to pull ahead, but Jeremy was going second and had a trivial time catching up on the final turn. Jeremy was a good opponent, and played a solid game.

I'd end up losing 81-88, a 9-11 loss. Not too bad, and keeping it close was my goal here. Our team would end up winning 94-66, thanks to big wins from Campbell, Wallace, and Goatboy. Campbell had to play Custodes three straight rounds and won two of those games big. He was a huge value add this year. That put us at 2-0-3 and in a pretty good spot - we'd absolutely improved on last year's 2-2-2 result.

Lunch was even easier today and I grabbed a gyro bowl from a food truck which was largely fine. It was filling, and that was what I needed at the time. Then we met up for our final round, which was absolutely fated to happen.

Round 6: vs. Sanctum (Astra Militarum)

LET'S FUCKING GOOOOOOOOO

I know a lot of people who rankle at the prospect of traveling to an event to play their friends. These people are wrong and dumb; I love playing against my friends, and I do it all the time.

We initially offered Sanctum a draw - let's just call it, play some games for funsies, and go home. A podium finish was possible for both teams but extremely unlikely. We were happy to merely go undefeated. But I could see the gears turning behind the more competitive Sanctum faces: They wanted to win, and thought we were beatable. So they declined our offer and we paired up.

Round 6 vs. Andrew Corban

And in a prodigious development, I got paired into Andrew Corban! Andrew and I played a practice game on the prior Monday (Labor Day), and so I was familiar with his list. He's not a blowout win guy on the team, but neither am I. This is the most chill game of Warhammer I've ever played at an event. Just hanging out, casual takebacks, nice trash talk, jokes, beers. Great times. Andrew is a 10/10 person.

Andrew's list has lots of medium sized tanks but he's on Recon so my goal is to Consecrate early, slow him by a turn, and kill his action units. That's hard, because killing Gaunt's Ghosts is really difficult and they can just jump around on the table. The plan here is to just score early and often and try to squeeze out 11 or 12 points in a win. I'm going second, which is a big help for scoring.

Andrew has a few scout moves, but spends his first turn playing cagey. As a result, I don't get to kill anything - my shooting up top goes disastrously - but I whittle a few things down during the turn I can capitalize on and I get needlessly aggressive with a turn 1 advance and charge from the Mutalith, which does nothing except end up giving me a dead Mutalith the following turn. Not my strongest strategic play, to be honest.

I picked up a couple of units on the following turn for a triple consecrate. That was a big deal, and this was all powered by a successful 9" charge out of deep strike with one of my Scarab units, which more or less sealed this game as a win for me.

Those Scarabs spent the next three turns getting killed by Leman Russes but managed to hold on long enough to be annoying, while the other Scarab brick dropped midtable and got to operate more or less unmolested for the rest of the game. Andrew and I had some fun back-and-forth while his final Kasrkin unit stayed locked in combat with my Forgefiend, refusing to die. This was bad for Andrew, however - he wanted to use the Reinforcements Stratagem to get the unit back, and so eventually had to do so by overcharging a plasma pistol and letting his model die from a failed Hazardous roll.

I'd end up pulling the Tzaangors across the table late to score Plunder and Outflank, but this left my home open for Gaunt's Ghosts to triangulate a third time. They were Andrew's beacon unit, and I tried taking them out with a Tzaangor Shaman + my Forgefiend, but wasn't able to make it happen - Gaunt re-rolled his final invulnerable save and stayed alive on 2 wounds, helping Andrew close the gap. I'd catch up on my final turn, but that essentially kept it from being a 14-6. I'd win 13-7, more than I expected after Monday's practice game and very solid.

Either way, it was a fun game. Andrew fuckin' rules. One of my favorite people.

And after all that, we tied with Sanctum anyways - Kelling, Wallace, and Shane scored big wins, Goatboy kept his game to a tie, and Campbell and Craig managed to score a few points to avoid a 20-0 loss. Chase took a big 20-0 loss here from Conor but that was honestly fine; Conor was playing the busted Dark Angels speeder build and Chase had our weakest Disruption list. Putting Conor into Chase was honestly a pairings mistake for Sanctum; we were already set to eat a big loss for Chase. This was our only points loss of the event - 79-18 - but still a tie by event standards.

UNDEFEATED, BABY!!!

Finishing 2-0-4 is very respectable and we ended in 14th place. That's very, very good for a team with no practice time or ability to coordinate in person and a cobbled-together set of lists. We're all stoked about this result and heading home as champions. Mrs. Kelling is on hand to help us do a single ride back, which is a massive upgrade.

Our final night is pasta night. I take a pound of ground pork and a pound of ground beef (season with salt, pepper, and Italian seasoning), and brown them in a pain before draining. We'd accidentally used all the garlic the night before on the mashed potatoes, but I still had a healthy ball of garlic rosemary butter and so I cooked up some small diced celery and carrots in that before adding the browned meat back in with a can of tomato paste. Let that cook a bit, then add water and once it cooks a bit, some heavy cream. It's not amazing as a bolognese - it needs another two hours to simmer with some wine - but the taste is absolutely there and it goes great on both the cheese tortellini I've bought and Campbell's lentil pasta (gluten free). We combine it with a Caesar salad and croutons and parmesan cheese for an incredibly solid meal. Chase got regular marinara sauce.

Chase's hair was going crazy

We drank and talked and recapped another successful teams weekend, satisfied with our results. We largely brought a bunch of off-meta or suboptimal lists and through sheer force of will managed an undefeated result. Chase had the worst go of it, losing every single game over the weekend with his Disruption Emperor's Children. I don't think it was a good list but when you chase your off-meta dreams, sometimes you fly too close to the sun and get burned.

The final night is always bittersweet, especially when people leave early. Kelling and his wife skipped dinner to go do vacation stuff. Craig, Campbell, Wallace, and Shane bounced early to catch late flights back home. Which left me, Chase, and Goatboy to clean up and lock down the house before leaving on Monday morning. The good news is I slept better that night and the next morning we were ready to go by check-out at 11am. We made the trip to the airport together, got some breakfast, and said our goodbyes.

Final Thoughts

Phew! What a great time - that was a lot to write about. Next week's update is bound to be pretty light - I don't think I'll have time to get a game in - but I'm going to try and get some hobby progress in the mix there. I had a blast at Challengers Cup this year - almost enough fun to want to do it again next year. I'm on the fence, mostly because the logistics behind 8-man teams events makes them a serious pain in the ass, even when the event is loads of fun. I know I'm definitely doing LVO Teams in February next year. After that, I'm less certain.

See you Thursday.

title: Two of the greatest D&D dungeons of all time are part of a new Humble Bundle with 95% discount
content:
For some time now, Humble Bundle has been putting together massive bundles of Goodman Games' Dungeon Crawl Classics and Dungeons & Dragons 5e books, letting you pick up an entire library of years' worth of adventuring for a fraction of the normal price. They're brilliant, and we've covered a lot of them - but this one is special. Offering $870 worth of books and maps for 40 bucks (95% discount, math fans) is par for the course here - but this bundle has just a little bit more sparkle.

That's because the headline products in the mix are two beloved, vintage dungeons, both originally written by the legendary Jennell Jaquays and published by Judges Guild in 1979. In both cases, the Humble Bundle includes both of Goodman Games' modern revivals of the dungeon: the D&D 5e version, and the port for Goodman's own popular OSR (old school revival) RPG system, Dungeon Crawl Classics (DCC).

Caverns of Thracia is an enormous, six level, 150+ encounter megadungeon that promises a year's worth of gameplay, taking your party from 1st to 10th level (or levels one to five in DCC) - and the vibes are just unspeakably good. Just read this excerpt from its description, via Humble:

"Born in the forgotten chambers and caverns of age-lost Thracia rises a formidable foe, the Minotaur King, along with his host of dogfolk, gnolls, lizardfolk and others. Some say Death itself lingers in the Caverns of Thracia, ready to claim any who stumble on its unholy chapel."

Sorry, Wizards of the Coast - but you just don't make 'em like they used to.

Hellpits of Nightfang, also by the incomparable Jaquays (though originally written for Chaosium's RuneQuest rather than D&D) is closer to the the adventure concepts modern players may be more used to. A town is being terrorized by "nocturnal attacks" from an unseen evil they call the Nightfang, and your party of 9th level heroes (5th level in the DCC version) have to investigate three local sinkholes - charmingly named "Hellpits" - to track down the "ferocious vampire" lurking within the lost hero's tomb beneath, and stake the bastard for good.

Like a lot of Goodman's revamped classic adventures, these books are oozing with the high concept fantastical heroics, campy aesthetics, and terrifyingly lethal enemies that characterize the OSR scene - and remember, it's not just those two dungeons you're getting for your 40 bucks here.

This bundle also packs in over 50 other items, including:

  • 12 more DCC adventure books.
  • Six more 5e conversion adventure books.
  • Two different versions of the DCC core rulebook (one with an alt art cover).
  • Four source books, content collections, and anthologies.
  • A stack of Goodman Games annuals and Gen Con program guides, with original art in.
  • A handful of map packs, token packs, and other goodies.

It's a banging deal, a prodigious library upgrade for any OSR fellow traveller, and - of course - because it's a Humble Bundle, a share of the profits goes to a charity: in this case the Make-A-Wish Foundation.

You'll already have heard of Make A Wish, it funds and organises fantastic experiences for children going through serious, life threatening illnesses. It's a good cause, and a good reason to go for this excellent bundle if you're on the fence.

Personally, my experience with OSR is limited to a few dips into the Borg-Verse, but the more I look at Goodman's old school D&D re-releases, and indeed DCC itself, the more tempted I get to give it a go. If you've already played any of these classic adventures (in their Goodman forms, or in Jaquays' original versions for D&D or RuneQuest) come join the free Wargamer Discord community and tell me more about them! I would genuinely LOVE to hear your tales of adventure.

title: Trench Crusade Warband Focus: The Red Brigade
content:
Welcome everyone to another Trench Crusade Warband focus! This week we round out the New Antioch with everyone’s favourite crimson warriors: The Red Brigade. Prepare for a story of grief, revenge, and the goodest of doggos. 

Credit: Westfalia Miniatures

The Lore

The Red Brigade is comprised of volunteers who share a common grief: The grief of loss. All members, from the very founding by St. Ernest, have experienced a profound loss as a result of the Great War. All members wear armour tarnished with the blood of a fallen comrade as proof of a “Blood Pledge.” Under the direct command of the Duke, before they set out on the most dangerous missions that regular units cannot do, they dine with the Duke and the elite in the “Feast of the Dead Men.” To be a member of the Red Brigade is to know your life is at its end. Reality simply needs to catch up with the inevitable truth.

The Variant

Before we get into things, let’s quickly break down the Variant’s rules: 

  • Displeasure of the Church: You may only bring up to one Trench Cleric and one Sniper Priest, or up to two Sniper Priests and no Trench Clerics. 
  • Fury of the Saint Ernest: Your Lieutenant may purchase the “Gunslinger” Skill (found in the post-game skill section) for 5 Ducats. Additionally, this warband may purchase Molotov Cocktails for 5 Ducats, but may not have a Troop Flag.
  • Glory Hounds: You may purchase Trench Dogs of the Red Brigade, and any Trench Dog bought in a campaign via Glory becomes a Trench Dog of the Red Brigade. You cannot have more Trench Dogs than other models, and the first two Glorious Deeds performed by a Trench Dog of the Red Brigade give 2 Glory Points, instead of 1. 
  • No Retreat: No model may perform Retreat, unless a special rule forces them to do so. 
  • Remember the Fallen: You may skip the Reinforcement and Exploration post-game steps in a Campaign to recover all possessions of models that died as a result of the Trauma step. 
  • Wear and Tear: You start the game with 1 Blood Marker per 200 Ducats of the total cost of the Warband. The opposing player distributes the Blood Markers however they like, with the stipulation that each model must have 1 Blood Marker on them before a 2nd can be applied. 

Before we get into what this all means, there are a couple of important rules to this variant that aren’t directly in the rule changes: A “Crimson Communicant,” which is a new (albeit a variant of) Communicant style Tough model. 

All in all, what we have is a strong, campaign-focused variant that can quickly snowball Glory acquisition through the clever use of Trench Dogs. Sure, the Wear and Tear rule is a downside, but it can be negated with medi-kits (*cough* Med Dogs *cough*). There aren’t many non-campaign-focused rule changes, but a big highlight is the Gunslinger ability for your Lieutenants, pushing them to an aggressive dual-pistol-wielding maniac on the board.  

Unique Battlekit

Blood Cloak - 5 Ducats - Limit: 4

A simple piece of Equipment that gives the wearer the Skirmisher Keyword. Skirmisher has some niche uses, and can help get you out of a potential charge, but is often unreliable. Still, nice and cheap piece of kit, if you really want to give an extra bit of survivability to something important, even if it won’t always help. 

Red Banner - 2 Glory - Limit: 1

A replacement for the lost Troop Flag, this 1-handed Flag gives the Block and Held Keywords, but also grants a +2 to Morale checks as long as the bearer is not Down or Out of Action. 

Key Units

Lieutenant 

Credit: Westfalia Miniatures

As always in any New Antioch warband, your Lieutenant is your key model, with fantastic combat stats, and great activation shenanigans. In Red Brigade, your Lieutenant is able to grab the Gunslinger skill for just 5 Ducats, which allows them to make two shooting actions if they have are weapons with the Pistol Keyword. If you immediately thought, “the Automatic Pistol has the Pistol Keyword,” then you’re right on the money, as a Lieutenant with double Automatic Pistols can shoot both of them in ranged Combat. 

Ideal Starting Loadout:
  • Automatic Pistol, Automatic Pistol
  • Standard Armour

Trench Dogs of the Red Brigade

Credit: Westfalia Miniatures

As the bestest of friends, as well as demanders of pets, Trench Dogs are usually useful units to pad out your model count, as well as cheap screeners to disrupt infiltrating units getting a useful position. However, in Red Brigade, you can pick from a bunch of useful abilities to make each of your four-legged friends more unique and useful to your playstyle. The Trench Dogs of the Red Brigade may have Grenades or Molotov Cocktails for 5 Ducats (more on that later). 

For basic abilities, we start with Dogs of War, which stipulates that your Dogs can’t be promoted, but do count towards Morale Checks. Next up is Four Paws, which grants a +1 Dice to Climbing, Jumping, Falling, or making a Dash, which is very useful on an 8” movement model. Next up is Grenade Harness, which allows other Non-Trench Dog models to make a Shoot Action as long as they are within 1” of a Trench Dog model with this ability. Loyal Hound allows up to two Trench Dogs of the Red Brigade, along with up to two non-Trench Dog models, to form a fireteam. Each Trench Dog must be with a Non-Trench Dog model. These two Fireteams are in addition to the regular Fireteams, and you can still use the Concentrated Attack ability. For the last of the regular abilities, Teeth and Claws allows a Trench Dog of the Red Brigade to make a melee attack without needing a Melee Weapon.

For the Special Training ability, you have to give each Trench Dog one of the following abilities for a 5 Ducat cost:

  • Attack Dog: +1 Dice to the Melee Characteristic
  • Guard Dog (Limit: 1): Enemy infiltrators cannot be deployed within 16” of an enemy Guard Dog unit. Additionally, it may charge an enemy model it cannot see. 
  • Mercy Dog (Limit: 2): Mercy Dogs may use medi-kits. Additionally, as long as the Mercy Dogs start their movement in contact with a friendly model, they may move that model along with them when the Trench Dog makes a normal move, reducing the movement by half when doing so, as long as the other friendly model is outside of 1” of an enemy unit.

Ok, so that is a lot to take in, but putting it all together, it makes your doggos incredibly useful, allowing them to fill in as speedy utility pieces that can block off parts of the board to your opponent, or act as a potential setup unit as part of a Fireteam. These are a great unit to have in your pocket, and at just 35 Ducats for the base, it’s a nice unit to have.

Crimson Communicant

Credit: Westfalia Miniatures

If getting a pair of small companions wasn’t enough of a reason to join the Red Brigade, what about a large (but equally cuddly?) companion? Crimson Communicants join the grim Red Brigade to help forget the loss and despair they feel, able to channel the sorrow of the Second Meta-Christ through the power of the Atonement Bell they always carry. 

The Crimson Communicant comes in at 75 Ducats, and has the regular 6” move, a -1 Ranged Characteristic, and a +1 Melee Characteristic. They are Elite and have the Strong and Tough keywords. Their special ability is Strength through Pain, where they gain a +1 to their Melee Characteristic for each Blood Marker they have. Secondly, an enemy cannot spend Blood Markers to add - Dice to a success roll for a Melee Attack Action. 

As mentioned, they come with the Atonement Bell, which is a 1-handed weapon they always have. A Crimson Communicant may use the Bell to make an off-hand attack that moves an enemy model D3”, instead of making an injury roll. The movement must be in a straight line, and can be used to make them fall, retreat, climb, jump, etc. You can’t use the Bell on a retreating model.

Whilst the Bell is a nice-to-have, it does take a 1-handed slot, so that means no shield-and-weapon combo. However, getting another model with Tough in this warband is fantastic. 

Ideal Starting Loadout: 
  • Two-handed Hammer
  • Standard / Reinforced Armour 
  • Medi-kit

The List 

Red Dawn

Faction: The Red Brigade

Rating: 699 Ducats | 0 Glory

Patron: None

## Elites ##

Lieutenant - 130D

Upgrades & Choices: Gunslinger

Battlekit: Automatic Pistol, Automatic Pistol, Standard Armour

Crimson Communicant - 105D

Battlekit: Atonement Bell, Great Hammer/Maul, Medi-Kit, Standard Armour

Sniper Priest - 69D

Battlekit: Pistol, Pistol, Frag Grenades

## Troops ##

Combat Engineer - 125D

Battlekit: Submachine Gun, Shovel, Engineer Body Armour, Satchel Charge

Mechanized Heavy Infantry - 120D

Battlekit: Heavy Shotgun, Reinforced Armour, Satchel Charge

Yeoman - 60D

Battlekit: Flamethrower

Yeoman - 50D

Battlekit: Musical Instrument, Molotov Cocktail

Guard Dog - 40D

So this list has a lot up front and doesn’t utilise a lot of cheap Dogs, but for me personally, I would rather bring my expensive units up front and acquire my cheaper units further down the line. We do have our three Elites, as well as the icon Combat Engineer and MHI combo. Lastly, with a single yeoman with a Flamethrower, we can at least tickle our opponents. Lastly, our cheap chaff is a Yeoman that can still contribute if needed with the cheap Molotov Cocktail, and the Guard dog is to stop early Infiltrator shenanigans.

As the campaign goes on, you can get cheap Attack Dogs to complement your other units, as well as get another Yeoman with a Flamethrower to make another power pair. 

Final Thoughts

The Reg Brigade is an incredibly unique faction that really excels in Campaign play, thanks to the use of Trench Dogs gaining you more glory. The Wear and Tear rule, whilst quite a hindrance, simply balances out the sheer amount of snowballing you can achieve whilst in a campaign. The use of Trench Dogs, as well as a larger Communicant model, adds a lot of versatility to your list, allowing you to approach games in some refreshing ways that can’t be found in other variants. All in all, the Red Brigade is great for Campaign players who love the core New Antioch formula but are looking to diversify how they approach their games.

title: Steamforged fans accuse the board game publisher of ignoring backers
content:
In 2024, UK-based game maker Steamforged Games (SFG) purchased the miniature wargame Warmachine, reviving the ailing game's fortunes and steadily pivoting its business operations to make Warmachine the core of everything it does. But, in the last few months, even as Warmachine flourishes, official updates and communications on several of SFG's as yet unfulfilled board game crowdfunding campaigns have slowed significantly. It's led growing numbers of commenters to complain they're being ignored, with no communication from Steamforged about when they might get their pledge rewards, leaving some to worry that they're being abandoned entirely.

At the start of June, news emerged that Steamforged had made staff in various teams redundant, canning plans to launch any future board game crowdfunding campaigns and putting its whole back into Warmachine. The question that backers of unfulfilled crowdfunding campaigns want answered is: has the company still got the people in place to bring those games to completion?

I've contacted the team to ask about the games' progress, and for their comments on the drastic slowdown in campaign updates - but at press time I've had no response. We'll update this story when SFG gets back to us. In the meantime, though, reviewing the latest updates and comms on its nine outstanding board game campaigns does show the firm giving backers less information, less often, since early 2026.

Currently, the company has four fully-funded board game projects for which it's still developing the game and product, and five where development work is complete, but printing or shipping some or all of the product isn't. The campaigns nearing completion received regular monthly updates in 2025, but in 2026 these have become irregular,

The last update to the crowdfunding campaigns for still-to-be-delivered projects Euthia: Cruel Frost, Horizon Forbidden West: Seeds of Rebellion, Monster Hunter World Iceborne, and Hearts of Iron all came on July 29. In each case the update was an apology for the lack of substantive information about when copies would be delivered, stating that the team was waiting for key information from partners.

There are a lot of customer comments on those updates, and I've not been able to find any responses from Steamforged. In the general comments areas for those crowdfunding campaigns, the only comment from Steamforged I've been able to find in the last six months was in the Iceborne Kickstarter in June, apologizing for the lack of a substantive update.

In December 2025 Steamforged launched a dedicated Warmachine community Discord, with staff moving from the studio's original community Discord to there. The last comment I can find by a member of staff in the old Discord was senior designer Jamie Perkins on July 31, explaining that he and his team had long since completed their work on Monster Hunter World: Iceborne, saying "the folks who can help are not active in the Discord server or the Facebook group. Information will only be shared by those folks on the official campaign page where everyone will be able to see it".

Without moderation, we get to see the worries and angers from the community writ large: fears that projects will never be delivered, and frustration at the lack of communication. On September 1 the UK's registrar for companies published a notice that Steamforged was on track to be dissolved as a company. SFG stated that this was a purely administrative issue caused by late submission of financial reports, and the registrar cancelled the notice on September 5. But in those four days the news spread like wildfire through the comment threads on the unfulfilled Kickstarters, apparently reflecting a community ready to believe that the firm was in big trouble.

One high profile project is now being delivered to fans. On September 9, Steamforged posted an update to the Gamefound page for 6 Siege: The Board Game, stating that copies in China, Australia, and New Zealand were shipping to backers; US and UK copies had arrived in each country, and address confirmation emails were being sent to backers; the vessel containing EU copies had docked but not yet unloaded; and for "all other regions, pledges are in transit and we expect fulfilment to begin at the end of this month or in October ".

Elden Ring: Rot and Sorcery, Bardsung - Tale of the Forsaken Glade, are both still in development, and their last updates came in June. Helldivers 2: The Board Game had an update in August, and Terra Mystica: Definitive Edition received an update on September 8.

Board game fulfilment is a notoriously slow process. But with the collapse of prominent crowdfunding studios such as Mythic Games and CMON, customers have a lower tolerance than ever for uncertainty.

Silence from Steamforged may reflect the remaining board game staff putting their now reduced capacity into working on games rather than talking about them, while Steamforged's comms staff are completely occupied with Warmachine. Or the most apocalyptic fears of the community could be true. I've asked Steamforged for an update about the actual situation, and will inform you when I receive one.

For a recent commentary on how split focus can cause delays and miscommunication for crowdfunding campaigns, check out my interview with Dave Nordquist from MiniWarGaming about the Ravaged Star crowdfunding campaign.

title: Tabletop Battles Reviews: The Wicked and the Warped, by Robert Rath
content:
Image credit: Games Workshop

Have you ever disliked something you read in a book so much that you physically took it out on the book itself?

I've done that exactly once in my life, but it's as fresh as yesterday. Growing up in the 80's, my childhood crush was Daryl Hannah after seeing her play a mermaid in 1984's Splash. Two years later she starred in The Clan of the Cave Bear as an orphaned Cro-Magnon woman, Ayla, taken in by a tribe of Neanderthals. Adolescent me found the story so compelling that I dove right into Jean M. Auel's book that the film was adapted from.

I progressed smoothly though the Earth's Children series, hopping from The Clan of the Cave Bear into The Valley of Horses- before running into trouble of the worst kind with The Mammoth Hunters. See, the second book of the series had introduced us to another Cro-Magnon, Jondalar, who served as Ayla's love interest after she had departed the tribe of Neanderthals. The two travel alone together for a time, before meeting the titular mammoth-hunting tribe in the third book. There, Ayla gets her head turned by brash ivory-carver Ranec, and when she succumbs to his charms and sleeps with him I was so incensed that I hurled the book across my room.

It rested there for three days before I was grudgingly able to resume the story.

I've had issues with other books over the years, but none have ever been quite so visceral as that one (ahh, youth). I found Robert Heinlein's second-half Stranger in a Strange Land transition so disagreeable that for months I was tempted to split the book in two and toss the back half into the rubbish bin, though a feeling for the sacredness of the art form stayed my hand. Throwing in a moment of volatility might be okay, but willfully damaging was off-limits.

It would take me many years more to begin to learn that just because I didn't like the choices and author had made doesn't necessarily mean that those were bad choices. Auel's love triangle powered much of The Mammoth Hunters through to its conclusion, delivering a tremendous payoff when Ayla chooses to continue journeying with Jondalar rather than remaining in the camp with Ranec. Stranger in a Strange Land's somewhat controversial mid-book pivot certainly didn't stop it from winning the prestigious Hugo Award in 1962.

And similarly, Robert Rath's choices in The Wicked and the Warped may not have been ones I enjoyed, but by no means does that make it a bad book.

Image credit: Games Workshop

The Story

The Wicked and the Warped begins when an ancient Necron world once lost to the Warp reappears in realspace following the rend in the galaxy caused by the Great Rift. Having marinaded in the immaterium for millennia, it immediately attracts the attention of Trazyn when it begins broadcasting a distress signal.

Trazyn, of course, sees ripe opportunity to acquire items of historical significance. Though a deeply skeptical Orikan shows little interest in accompanying him, when the matter rises to the attention of Triarch Praetorian Executor Phillias (also returning from the first book) it quickly becomes a group expedition- willing or otherwise.

That group- accompanied by a human Inquisitor plucked from suspended animation in Trazyn's galleries as a sort of canary in the coal mine for warp sensitivity- finds a world filled with the remnants of Necron civilization, yet also indelibly suffused with the essence of Chaos. As their expedition gets mired deeper and deeper in this surreal and mysterious world, can they discover what's really happened to the world of Amenthis in time to make it back out again?

The Sophomore Slump

As I discussed in my recent review of The Infinite and the Divine's Illustrated and Annotated Edition, the book was Rath's debut novel in 2020 and its resultant success was by no means assured. Thinking there was a good chance he might not get a second book offer from the Black Library, he swung for the fences with that one- and connected. The combination of historical-centered drama combined with a delightful comedic element proved such a hit with readers that it eventually dethroned none other than Dan Abnett's Horus Rising to take the '#1 book' shelf at Warhammer World.

While Rath has written two other novels since, with 2022's Assassinorum: Kingmaker followed the next year by The Fall of Cadia, he almost certainly faced a different kind of pressure in writing the return of everyone's favorite Necron 'odd couple,' Trazyn the Infinite and Orikan the Diviner. In short, how do you recapture the magic?

This question has haunted creatives for as long as people have been creating. and it's probably safe to assume that the unlikelier the initial success, the greater the pressure can be to avoid the dreaded 'sophomore slump.' For every The Godfather Part II, there's at least one (if not more) Southland Tales; for every The Bends by Radiohead there's another like MGMT's Congratulations. If, as Princess Irulan notably observes in Frank Herbert's Dune, a "beginning is a difficult time," a follow-up is no walk in the park either.

Imagine what this was like for Rath as he sat down at his writing desk for The Wicked and the Warped the first time. While obviously no party to his internal deliberations, I imagine with regards to the book's tone they may broadly have gone something like this: with the first book a dramatic story with comedic elements, do you...

  1. Lean into the drama a bit more
  2. Lean into the comedy a bit more
  3. Try and strike roughly the same balance as you did the first time

While past results are never a guarantor of future performance, we can probably assume that the third option there- dancing with the one you came with- is generally the safest best. So with that being said, I give Rath a lot of credit for picking the option I would have assumed to be the biggest gamble: option number two.

And boy does it lean in.

Image credit: Games Workshop

Laugh til' You Cry

Comedy in 40K isn't quite the no-man's land as we see with romance, but it's probably fair to call it a distant second. You have the Orks, of course, Sandy Mitchell's Commissar Cain, and then... well, that's pretty much it, right? That isn't to say that the grim, dark future doesn't have moments of humor (our early introduction to Guardsman Hawke in Graham McNeill's Storm of Iron certainly comes to mind), but humor and comedy aren't the same thing.

The Infinite and the Divine was a masterpiece, not least because of how deftly Rath managed to weave its elements together into an extraordinary whole. From Orikan's use of rewound time to rig up a tribunal hearing in his favor to Trazyn's Catachan "gift" for his rival, the book's hilarity was often clever, subtle, and often unexpected. I still occasionally chuckle when I recall the scene I mentioned in my review:

"I'm being deliberately vague here to avoid any spoilers for the new reader, but perhaps my favorite example here was when Trazyn- who is able to shift his consciousness into other, lesser Necron- masquerades as one of Orikan's soldiers, affecting a deliberate slowness and stupidity sure to trigger the intellectual snobbishness of his rival. It's side-splittingly funny watching Orikan grow increasingly exasperated and on-tilt, but only because Rath has put in the work throughout the book of showing Orikan's smartest-guy-in-the-room arrogance."

Those wanting more of the same in The Wicked and the Warped may well end up disappointed. Rather than longer-buildup humor, Rath plays in a much more immediate, slapstick space that frequently inviked the animations of my youth, from Tom & Jerry to Looney Tunes. If you've ever seen two characters fighting over an item, with one of them grabbing it before running away in the opposite direction only to run into a low-hanging tree branch when they turn to stick their tongue out at their rival, well, you'll know exactly what I mean here. In fact, something very close to this exact gag occurs early in the book.

In another moment, Trazyn gets Orikan to look down a hole before shoving him in. Later- in a gag that immediately brought Daffy Duck to mind- Orikan gets ready to charge an enemy. Trazyn, channeling classic Bugs Bunny in turn, has his 'I wouldn't do that if I were you' moment, Orikan ignores him, then jumps back to safety moments later shot up and trailing black smoke.

But perhaps most of all, the constant squabbling between the two seemed to border on Flanderization, a topic I recently went into some detail on in my audiobook review of Sandy Mitchell's Death or Glory. Part of the problem is simply down to the book's narrative structure.

In The Infinite and the Divine, Orikan and Trazyn spent as much of the book apart as they did together. The jabs and needling, then, were funny because the humor had room to breathe. Rath's decision to pair the two together for nearly the entirely of The Wicked and the Warped means that the pacing of their interaction seldom gets a reprieve. They're together all the time, so there's no room for elaborate schemes or breaks between squabbling interactions. Imagine having dinner with a witty, sarcastic couple who enjoys taking the piss out from one another as a form of entertainment. Then try to imagine spending a week camping with them.

Image credit: Games Workshop

So What Worked?

This wasn't the book that I was hoping for when it was announced, but Robert Rath is an exceptional writer and there were still plenty of things that worked here- even if (for me) they couldn't quite escape the shadow of what didn't.

For one thing, I really enjoyed how Rath looked to showcase a different side of the two characters by hobbling their strengths. We saw plenty of Orikan's temporal shenanigans and Trazyn's ability to shift bodies in the first book; here, Rath forces them to have to go without recourse to those powers for much of the story given the nature of the realm they're in. This was canny storycrafting, deftly avoiding painting himself into the proverbial corner in a way that made total sense for the narrative and allowing him to peer with his author's eye into other elements of the characters.

There were also some genuinely terrific passages when Rath allowed his characters to connect with one another on a deeper level. A conversation between Trazyn and Orikan on consciousness and time travel dove into the metaphysical left me wanting more of these kinds of discussions, and passages dealing with dreaming and the nature of the soul gave the book a glimpse of the depth its predecessor enjoyed.

"That was one aspect I really wanted to explore in this book," he notes in the Special Edition's introduction, "how Orikan's ability to manipulate time makes him alienated and cynical... He carries the scars of all these abandoned timelines, having experienced every insult and slight that some alternate version of Trazyn has thrown at him."

"With Trazyn," he continues, "I was interested in digging into how divorced he feels from the galaxy. His soullessness keeps him from authentically experiencing life and belonging, while his immortality and sense of time forces him into the role of an observer in a galaxy that's passed him by."

There are also some terrific Easter eggs and clever touches in here, particularly as we get a look at Trazyn's collections. An offhand (and hilariously irreverent) reference to Voyager and its Golden Record. One of the last statues in existence of one of the purged primarchs. Scarabs killing their foes with heat like honeybees. A cameo from a larger-than-life figure from one of his past novels.

Rath has one of the best "attention to detail" eyes in the modern Black Library, and in particular the sequences in Trazyn's gallery on Solemnace had the same "blink and you'll miss a reference" feeling I associate most strongly with Robert Anton Wilson's Illuminatus! Trilogy. You also see some of this in the way that Rath masterfully manages to tie in the first book to the second, but not in a way you'd ever expect.

Final Thoughts

Even if ultimately The Wicked and the Warped didn't click for me, I was heartened to see how much enjoyment people have been sharing from reading this one in the usual Black Library watering holes. Just as with Marc Collins's Eidolon, the Auric Hammer (which placed second in the Black Library Book of the Year for 2024), it's a good reminder that just because I didn't enjoy a book doesn't mean that others won't- and it certainly doesn't mean that the book is bad.

If there's a lament, it's that I'd have tremendously enjoyed a book where we were able to better explore the inner workings of both Orikan and Trazyn- as Rath noted in the introduction- without the distraction of the dialed-up silliness.

Given the book's ending, it seems highly likely that we're now two-thirds of the way through a trilogy, with (at least) one more Trazyn/Orikan book forthcoming. I'll be keen to see which direction he ends up leaning for it, and whether it will be more like this book or a return to the more balanced approach of The Infinite and the Divine.

As long as neither one shacks up with a Cro-Magnon ivory carver, I'm sure I'll be okay.

title: Wizards says MTG Reality Fracture's 'Jace' card is an "intentional call back", not art copying
content:
On Wednesday, Wizards of the Coast revealed the deck list for the upcoming Reality Fracture Commander deck, Reality Reforged, and its powerful new commander, a four color variant of Jace Beleren called Jace, Multiverse Architect. Immediately, fans began to notice that the card's art, illustrated by Volkan Baga, had key motifs that were suspiciously similar to the popular sorcery card Breach the Multiverse, illustrated by Liiga Smilshkalne. But, on Friday, Baga and Wizards of the Coast provided Wargamer with a joint statement saying the new art is a "direct, intentional call back", but not a copy-and-paste job.

In these pictures I've mapped the art for Realmbreaker (the abstract energy pattern floating around Jace, Reality Architect) onto the same design in Breach the Multiverse, and there is a very clear resemblance between them.

If you want to try this for yourself, you can use the free graphic design software GIMP. Import a copy of the art for Breach the Multiverse and a picture of Jace, Reality Architect as two separate layers, with Jace on top. Set Jace's opacity to around 50% so you can see Breach the Multiverse underneath. I found it helpful to delete the parts of Jace's layer that weren't the Realmbreaker energy pattern so their shapes were a lot more obvious.

1/6

By rotating, rescaling, and repositioning Jace (but not actually warping or reshaping the fundamental image), you can quickly show that the shapes for each part of his Realmbreaker design map precisely onto the corresponding part on the earlier card.

It's not a one to one match - particularly, if you rescale Jace to get the bottom of the design to match, the top will be out of scale, and visa versa. And the card as a whole is almost entirely different except for this motif. Here's the joint statement from Wizards of the Coast and Volkan Baga on how the art was created:

"We've seen some of the discussion around the art of Jace, Multiverse Architect by Volkan Baga and Breach the Multiverse by Liiga Smilshkalne and wanted to make a few things clear.

First, the art direction given to Volkan was to directly reference this piece into the art. Much of the visual storytelling in Reality Fracture centers on Jace utilizing or incorporating powerful magic he has learned from events he has experienced. This was a direct, intentional call back to that moment to indicate that, in his efforts to rid the multiverse of Phyrexia, Jace had become the very thing he sought to eradicate.

Second, Volkan created this piece traditionally, from a first sketch done by hand up through the final painted version.

Finally, Magic has long created visual callbacks in its art to evoke connection through its shared multiverse. This has spurred some additional internal conversations about how we communicate those callbacks to artists who create iconic pieces, but it is very important to us to create a shared world that feels unified. This includes use of symbols, characters, and important moments throughout art.

We've been in contact with both artists and appreciate measured discussions around these important topics."

If you're interested in "measured discussions about important topics", you'll find a warm welcome in the Wargamer Discord community!

title: "Several pallets" of Pokemon 30th Celebration seemingly stolen in Delaware van heist
content:
It's hard to get your hands on Pokémon 30th Celebration anywhere, but if you're a resident of Smyrna, Delaware, things are even worse. On Thursday, the local and online retailer Safari Zone shared some very bad news to its Twitter followers: a truck containing "several pallets of 30th anniversary products" has disappeared from all communications, and they fear that it's been stolen.

If you're picturing a Team Rocket style heist involving a balloon and a giant grabbing claw picking the truck up off the road, well, so are we. But the truth is, the fate of the truck, and its cargo of extremely valuable Pokémon cards, is a mystery - we only know it "has still not delivered or been located".

"On Wednesday September 16 one of our [distributors] reached out to us asking if we had received the shipment", Safari Zone writes on Twitter. When they responded that it hadn't arrived, "the distro rep went into panic mode". The rep then reportedly told them "that the shipping company they used can not locate our delivery", which was apparently outsourced to an independent contractor with a privately owned truck.

Safari Zone was closed to locals on Thursday, which the statement says was "to do some serious math, and make sure all preorders were accounted for". It adds "all preorders will be honored and shipped… we just need some time". But "there will NOT be any restocks to offer any time soon" for online customers, and for locals "there will not be very much to offer".

Safari Zone states that "some information I can not share and some questions I will not be able to answer due to the active Police investigation". That includes the identity of the distributor and the total value of the missing items. It adds "we are working closely with our distro with this issue and preparing for the worse but still hoping for the best".

If you're lucky enough to be opening your packs right now, we'd love to see your hits in the Wargamer Discord community!

title: TheChirurgeon's Road Through 2026, Part 38: Days 1-2 of Challenger's Cup
content:
Welcome back, Dear Reader, to my ongoing blog of hobby and competitive play progress through 2026. Last week I was doing some final prep for Salt Lake City. And by "final prep" i mean "playing a lot of HeroQuest," though I did get in one extremely important practice game against my friend Andrew Corban on Labor Day. Anyways, this week I'm talking about the 2026 Challengers Cup. This is ostensibly four days of Warhammer - two travel days and three days of games - so I'm going to talk about Thursday and Friday today and then tomorrow I'll be back with an extra instalment to talk about days two and three of the event and the trip back. This will hopefully let me get a bit more "travel diary" about things and let some of the prose breathe. or something.

Anyways, here's ten thousand words about my Warhammer vacation with the boys.

Thursday: The Boys Return to Town

There are a limited number of direct flights from IAH to SLC every day, so I had to leave around midday and fly back Monday morning. That effectively turns this into a five-day event, which is a lot, especially if you aren't blessed with the boon of working from home and largely being able to just work from the airport and/or plane.

Also pictured (left to right): Erik Nelson, T Chambliss, Andrew Corban, and David Miracle

As luck would have it, I was on the same flight to Salt Lake City as Sanctum, the Houston team of local degenerates which makes up a large portion of my regular play group. We sat in the terminal and talked for a while, grabbing beers until it was time to board. Then our flight was delayed for mechanical reasons and we were deplaned. Then we were delayed due to lightning strikes - the tarmac shuts down when there's visible lightning in the area to protect workers - for another hour or so before we finally set out.

Once I arrived in Salt Lake City, I just had to wait for James "Boon" Kelling to pick me up - he'd rented a car. We had a great location for this event: 15 minutes from the airport, 15 minutes from the venue, which meant we could get away with a single car and make round trips to the venue/airport and back. Speaking of which...

The Team House

The house itself was a large house meant for ski trips. Whenever you do these 8-man team events, you always have two big challenges:

  1. The car. Unless you rent a bus or full size van, nothing is going to seat eight of you, especially once you start factoring in the space needed for armies and miniature cases. This usually means you have to rent two cars. Or do what we did and make two trips every time you go somewhere.
  2. The house. Finding a house which can sleep eight people who don't want to share a bed is nearly impossible. Even with big houses, you're usually talking four or five bedrooms at most, and maybe a couch or two. Which usually means someone has to sleep on the floor unless you have a lot of couches and/or fold-out beds.

When I book a house for something like this I'm usually looking for 5 bedrooms and 3 couches, or a fold-out bed or two. I also tend to focus on getting a decent kitchen and making sure we have a grill at the house. The grill makes cooking meals a lot easier, and one of the things I emphasize at teams events is doing big family-style dinners with cooked meals. We eat healthier, we eat cheaper, and we eat as a team.

This particular house had a solid grill and a great back patio with some truly amazing views. The landscape out in Salt Lake City is absolutely something, and it's a bit surreal when you're walking around and surrounded by mountains. On our way back to the house we stopped at the grocery store to do our preliminary grocery run. This is one of my favorite parts of any team or group vacation: I love planning meals and doing the grocery run. I feel like the quartermaster whenever I hit the grocery store on that initial run, sending runners to different aisles, investigating meat and picking fruit, doing it in absurd quantities - MY BOYS GOTTA EAT.

Dinner our first night was burgers and dogs. I biffed this a bit, in that Chase is a vegetarian and I didn't account for that, but he made do with the large variety of snacks, fruits, and vegetables on the first night, then on the second night we picked up some quick substitutions for him to ensure we had proper coverage. Burgers and dogs are usually my night 1 go-to; they're quick and easy, just do the burgs about 7 minutes per side on the grill with some salt and pepper, maybe some Montreal steak seasoning and worcestershire sauce if you wanna get fancy, and heat the dogs while you heat up some chili and cheese. Flip the burgers once.

We waited up for our final team member, Wallace, to arrive, and had a proper reunion chat and some beer before calling it a night. We spend some time on the porch and talk about lists, look at our round 1 pairing, and talk theory. As it turns out, Chase is a sicko who loves to do pairings, which is GREAT, because I hate doing pairings. I'm purely a vibes guy. And so is Chase, actually - he's just way better at it than I am. I end up crashing around midnight, with a dessert which consisted of "a fistful of pepto bismol."

Meet the Team

The Tabletop Battles team is not a traditional team for this kind of event; most of these teams are located near each other, or have players who can regularly practice. Our team is spread out all over, and no two players in our group have the ability to regularly play in person. This means we have zero hours of practice as a group, and have to largely rely on player skill to get through our matchups. the good news is, we're all at least decent players, and some of us are very good. Here's the rundown of the team we fielded this year, which is mostly the same as last year, but with two substitutions.

Robert "TheChirurgeon" Jones

Thousand Sons - Purge the Foe

Hey, it's me! I was ostensibly team captain of this outfit, but I handed those duties over to chase pretty quickly. My list for this event was pretty bad - designed to get Thousand Sons on Purge the Foe and pull off some bullshit tricks - more on that in a bit. I've been playing for a while, and just started elevating my game to winning GTs and attending WCW for the first time last year. I've done about half a dozen teams events now, including last year's Challengers Cup.

Chase "Gunum" Garber

Emperor's Children - Disruption

Chase was supposed to be on our team last year, but injured his hands pretty badly doing gardening work and had to take about half a year off of Warhammer as a result. He's one of the game's better list builders and an absolute pervert when it comes to doing pairings - he loves doing them, and basically cook over as team captain once we arrived at the event. Chase was running a very off-meta Emperor's Children army, focused on Flawless Blades.

James "Boon" Kelling

Aeldari - Priority Assets

Probably the most accomplished single player on the Tabletop Battles team, James has a long history of awards and strong play, having finished in the top 20 of the ITC multiple times and having won a World Championship in 2022 by taking down Andrew Gonyo in the Best Overall bracket. James has recently lost a bit of a step thanks to the selfish decision to "have children," but is always dangerous as he's just an incredibly smart player on the table.

Campbell "srm" McLaughlin

Space Marines - Take and Hold

Campbell is in a wonderful position of being a former casual/narrative player who has since been comp-pilled and as of last year, teampilled. Campbell is on Space Marines, and while his first competitive love are Black Templars, he's currently being forced to play Ultramarines for our team. He's on a list that uses Librarius Conclave and will likely end up having to take on Custodes in most of our matchups.

Shane Watts

Chaos Daemons - Take and Hold

Shane is another venerable veteran of the competitive scene, and was on last year's Ottawa and Challengers Cup teams. Shane's moved on from his Votann, and has recently been playing a Plague Legion list that specializes in battle-shocking you far past any notions of reason or restraint. He's packing a Sloppity Bilepiper because few things are as satisfying as killing Ghazghkull from a single failed Leadership test at -2.

Thomas "Goatboy" Reidy

World Eaters - Purge the Foe

Goatboy is back on the team this year for Challengers Cup, and he's once again packing World Eaters. Goatboy is one of my favorite people in this hobby, and he's a delight to have on the team. He's been on World Eaters for a while now, and was also playing them back in January during the LVO Teams Tournament. His list is Berzerker Horde; he's not about the fancy triple detachment tricks or running lots of Terminators.

Craig "MasterSlowPoke" Sniffen

Orks - Priority Assets

Our resident Rainbow Warriors sicko, MasterSlowPoke has recently been building an Orks army following the release of 11th edition. With the Codex out and legal for this event, he's well positioned to play one of the game's best armies, and we're super invested in having a top meta army or two in our team roster. The big challenge is that Craig has played exactly zero games with his army before this event. But when you have flash gitz, that shouldn't matter, right?

Wallace O'Donnell

Chaos Knights - Reconnaissance

Wallace is a chill dude and a lifesaver as far as I'm concerned. Last year he saved our asses by joining last minute after we had a drop, and he did the same thing this year after we had a player drop from the event with just a few weeks to go. That level of frustration normally makes my desire to do 8 man events bottom out, but I'm always happy to include Wallace, who's not only good for it, but an absolute list building genius who always comes up with cool shit. He's a very underrated player.
